entries.name: Chinese paper cutting
entries.origin_note: Developed in China after the invention of paper, with the earliest surviving examples from the Northern Dynasties period (5th to 6th century CE) and a continuous tradition since.
entries.summary: Chinese paper cutting, or jianzhi, is the art of making patterns and pictures by cutting folded or flat paper with scissors or a small knife. Paper was invented in China about two thousand years ago, and the oldest surviving paper-cuts, found in tombs at Turpan in Xinjiang, are symmetrical circles and animals from the fifth and sixth centuries. The art flourished under later dynasties, and was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009.
entries.how_played: The cutter folds a square of thin paper, often red, in half, quarters or more, so that the design repeats on unfolding. Cuts are made along the folded edges and into the body of the folded wedge using small sharp scissors or a knife, with a pattern drawn or mentally planned. A cut on a fold edge opens into a whole shape when the paper is unfolded, and a cut at the centre becomes the heart of the design. The cutter then opens the paper carefully to reveal the symmetrical pattern.
entries.heritage_note: Paper-cuts are pasted on windows and doors for the Spring Festival, given at weddings and birthdays and used as embroidery patterns, and each region has its own style. Cuts from Yu County in Hebei are coloured, cuts from northern Shaanxi are bold and expressive, and those from Foshan in Guangdong use metal foil. Typical subjects include flowers, fish, the twelve zodiac animals and characters of good fortune, with red the colour of luck. Skills are passed down within families, and especially from mothers and grandmothers to girls.

entries.name: Conkers
entries.origin_note: Recorded from the mid-1800s in England, the Isle of Wight is the earliest documented place. It grew out of older string games played with snail shells and hazelnuts, and it spread across Britain and Ireland wherever horse chestnut trees were planted.
entries.summary: Conkers is the autumn playground game of Britain and Ireland, played with the glossy brown seeds of the horse chestnut tree threaded on a length of string. Two players take turns to swing their conker at the other's until one of them shatters. The tree was brought to Britain from the Balkans in the late 1500s, and the first written account of children playing with the seeds comes from the Isle of Wight in 1848, where the game had earlier been played with snail shells and hazelnuts. Today it ends each September in organised championships as well as in every school yard.
entries.how_played: Each player drills a hole through a conker, threads it on a string about 25 centimetres long and knots the end. One player lets the conker dangle at arm's length while the other winds the string round their hand, pulls back and takes a swing at it. Players alternate strikes; if the strings tangle, the first to call out 'snags' gets a free strike. The last conker whole wins, and a conker that has beaten others inherits their tally, so a champion is a 'oner', a 'twoer' or a 'fiver' and counts every victory of the opponents it has beaten.
entries.heritage_note: Conkers belongs to the seasonal calendar of children in the United Kingdom and Ireland: the seeds fall in September and October, and the game lasts only as long as the supply. Folk wisdom is full of ways to make a champion, from baking and soaking in vinegar to keeping a conker for a full year, although organised events treat all such tricks as cheating and usually provide the conkers themselves. The World Conker Championships have been held every October since 1965 in Ashton, Northamptonshire, and raise money for charity. Health and safety debates, and a few school bans on the game, have become part of its modern story.

entries.name: Djembe
entries.origin_note: A Mande instrument from the Mali Empire region of West Africa, with its history before the 20th century known mainly through oral tradition.
entries.summary: The djembe is a goblet-shaped hand drum from West Africa, carved from a single piece of hardwood and covered with a goatskin head. It originated among the Mandinka (Maninka) and Bambara peoples of the old Mali Empire, today's Mali, Guinea and neighbouring countries. A familiar Maninka saying explains its name: 'anke djé, anke bé', meaning 'everyone gather together in peace'. Its sounds range from deep bass to ringing tone and sharp slap, which are all produced by the bare hands.
entries.how_played: The drummer wears the djembe from a strap or holds it between the knees and strikes the head with both hands. Striking the centre of the skin with the whole hand gives the deep bass, striking near the rim with the fingers together gives an open tone, and striking at the very edge with relaxed fingers gives the slap. In an ensemble the djembe players are joined by bass drums called dunun, and a lead drummer plays calls and solos over repeating patterns while accompanists hold the rhythm. The group answers, repeats and develops phrases in turn.
entries.heritage_note: In the Mande world, the making of drums traditionally belongs to the blacksmith families, and the drum is played at weddings, naming days, harvests and community celebrations as well as at big dances. Each rhythm, such as Kuku or Djole, is linked to a particular occasion, dance or group, and mastering the repertoire requires years of apprenticeship. In the 1950s the Guinean company Les Ballets Africains, founded by Fodeba Keita, brought the djembe to international stages, and drummers such as Mamady Keita and Famoudou Konate carried it around the world. Djembe circles are now found in cities across the globe.

entries.name: Juldarigi
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Classical Worlds (about 1000 BCE to 500 CE), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Japan and Korea.
entries.summary: Tug of war, two teams pulling on one rope, is among the oldest contests of strength and is played at village festivals from Korea and Japan to Britain and Indonesia; several Asian rope-pulling festivals are listed as living heritage.
entries.how_played: Teams grip the rope on either side of a centre mark and pull in time to a caller; the side that drags the mark past its own line wins. Rhythm, footing and holding the surge matter as much as weight.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of South Korea, United Kingdom, Indonesia.

entries.name: Koto
entries.origin_note: Introduced from China in the 7th and 8th centuries and developed in Japan into a distinct tradition, with its modern solo repertoire established in the 1600s.
entries.summary: The koto is the Japanese long zither, with thirteen silk strings stretched over a body of paulownia wood about 180 centimetres long and a movable bridge under each string. It was introduced from China during the Nara period, in the seventh and eighth centuries, together with the court music known as gagaku, and it developed its own solo and ensemble repertoire in Japan. The great blind composer Yatsuhashi Kengyo, in the seventeenth century, set the foundations of the modern koto tradition.
entries.how_played: The player kneels at the side of the instrument and plucks the strings with ivory picks, called tsume, worn on three fingers of the right hand. The movable bridges are set for the key of the piece before the performance, and the left hand presses the string behind a bridge to raise the pitch by a half or whole step. Players also sweep across the strings, strike them with the pick and slide to produce a wide range of tone colours. The koto is played solo, with voice and as part of the trio known as sankyoku with shamisen and shakuhachi.
entries.heritage_note: In the Edo period the koto was the instrument of the blind musicians' guilds and a mark of cultivation among women of the upper classes. In the twentieth century Miyagi Michio, whose Haru no Umi (Sea of Spring, 1929) is among the best-known Japanese pieces, joined the traditional koto with Western music and added the seventeen-string bass koto. Today it is heard at New Year celebrations, weddings and concerts, and is studied by amateur players of all ages.

entries.name: Origami
entries.origin_note: Developed in Japan from the 7th century onward after the arrival of paper; the first surviving instruction book dates from 1797, and the modern international art spread after the 1950s.
entries.summary: Origami is the Japanese art of folding a single sheet of paper into a figure, without cutting or gluing, and its name joins ori, 'fold', and kami, 'paper'. Paper reached Japan from China and Korea about the seventh century, and folded paper was used for ceremonial wrapping and decoration before it became a pastime. The first surviving book of folding instructions, Hiden Senbazuru Orikata, appeared in 1797, and it explains how to fold linked cranes from one sheet.
entries.how_played: The folder starts with a square of paper and makes a sequence of valley folds, where the paper folds toward the folder, and mountain folds, where it folds away. Creases are pressed sharp and the paper is reshaped by opening, flattening and turning steps, for example a squash fold or a reverse fold. The crane, with its long neck and spread wings, is the most famous model, and a kite, a fish and a paper dart are good starters. Each model is described by a short series of diagrams that follow the same set of symbols used worldwide.
entries.heritage_note: The modern art owes much to Akira Yoshizawa (1911-2005), who created thousands of designs and developed the system of lines and arrows now used in instruction diagrams, later refined with the Western folders Samuel Randlett and Robert Harbin. Paper folding also has independent traditions in China, Spain and Germany, where it was part of the kindergarten method of Friedrich Froebel. A thousand paper cranes, senbazuru, strung together are given in Japan as a wish for health and long life, and the crane has become a global symbol of peace. Modern folders explore mathematics, engineering and medical devices with the same craft.

entries.name: Oud
entries.origin_note: Developed in the Middle East from earlier lutes; written sources from the 9th century onward describe its tuning and use in the courts of Baghdad and Cairo.
entries.summary: The oud is the pear-shaped, short-necked, fretless lute at the heart of Arab and Middle Eastern music. Its name comes from the Arabic al-ud, 'the wood', and the same word is the source of the European word lute through Moorish Spain. The instrument is most closely associated with Iraq, Syria and Egypt, though it is also central to music in Turkey, Iran, the Maghreb and the Gulf. Its likely ancestor, the Persian barbat, is a few centuries older.
entries.how_played: The player sits with the oud resting across the lap and plucks with a plectrum held in the right hand, traditionally a long piece of eagle feather. The strings are arranged in pairs, called courses, usually eleven strings in total with a single bass string, and tuned in fourths. Since there are no frets, the left hand slides along the bare neck to find each note exactly, including the quarter-tones that give maqam modes such as Rast and Bayati their character. The player improvises melodic lines over rhythmic cycles, and often opens a performance with a free-form taqsim.
entries.heritage_note: The ninth-century Baghdad musician Ziryab is said to have taken the oud to Cordoba in Moorish Spain, where he added a fifth course of strings and helped found a school of music that shaped later Andalusian traditions. The philosophers al-Kindi and al-Farabi wrote about it, and the oud is sometimes called the king of instruments. In the twentieth century great players such as Munir Bashir of Iraq, Farid al-Atrash and Mohamed Abdel Wahab of Egypt and Riad al-Sunbati made it a solo instrument as well as an accompaniment for singers. Modern makers in Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo are renowned for carved sound holes and thin, bent-staved bowls.

entries.name: Rugby football
entries.origin_note: Developed at Rugby School in Warwickshire, England, in the early 1800s from older village football games that allowed handling the ball, and formalised in London in 1871.
entries.summary: Rugby football takes its name from Rugby School in Warwickshire, where a version of the football game with handling and running had taken hold by the 1820s; the old story that William Webb Ellis invented it by picking up the ball in 1823 first appeared decades later and is not supported by contemporary evidence. The Rugby Football Union was founded in London in 1871, and the sport soon spread through the British Empire to become a national passion in New Zealand and South Africa. The conversion kick, which gives two extra points after a try, is one of the sport's most watched moments of pure skill.
entries.how_played: After a try is scored, the scoring side may attempt a conversion kick from any point in line with where the ball was grounded, at any distance back from the try line. The ball is placed upright on a tee, and the kicker has a limited amount of time to take the attempt while the opposing team waits behind the try line. The ball must pass over the crossbar and between the two upright posts to count, and the kicker reads wind, distance and angle before a short, rehearsed run-up. A successful conversion is worth two points, and a try itself is worth five.
entries.heritage_note: Rugby union is played in more than a hundred countries and carries a strong sense of tradition: the ball itself is still named after the school town, and kickers such as those of the All Blacks and the Springboks are celebrated as national figures. In New Zealand and South Africa the sport is closely tied to community identity, school and club life, and to long-standing rivalries between the two nations. A separate code, rugby league, split away in northern England in 1895. A conversion attempt is known for its silence, as a stadium of tens of thousands falls quiet while the kicker makes a deliberate routine.

entries.name: Ski jumping
entries.origin_note: Developed in Norway in the 1800s, especially in the Telemark district, and carried abroad by Norwegian emigrants and sports-minded travellers in the late 1800s.
entries.summary: Ski jumping is a winter sport born in the snowy hills of Norway, where skiers jump from a ramp and are judged on both how far they fly and how cleanly they land. Competition jumping developed in the Telemark region in the 1800s, and Sondre Norheim of Morgedal became a legendary figure for his long jumps and his new style of binding. The first public jumping contests are recorded in the early 1860s, and the Holmenkollen hill above Oslo has hosted a national festival since 1892.
entries.how_played: The jumper crouches on the in-run of a long, icy track, picks up speed, and extends from the take-off lip into a flight position with the skis spread forward and apart in a V. Five judges award marks for style, taking points off for poor balance, bent skis in flight or a rough landing, and the distance is measured from the take-off to the landing. The jumper lands in the telemark pose, with one foot placed ahead of the other and the knees bent, and holds it to the end of the run-out. Points are then adjusted for wind and for the height of the starting gate.
entries.heritage_note: Ski jumping is a national passion in Norway and also in Finland, Austria, Germany, Poland, Slovenia and Japan. The telemark landing, named for the region where skiing was developed as a sport, is a living link to the earliest jumpers and is still required by the rules. The sport was part of the first Winter Olympic Games at Chamonix in 1924, and women's competitions joined the Olympic programme in 2014. The modern V-style, in which the skis are held apart in flight, was introduced by the Swedish jumper Jan Boklov in the 1980s and quickly replaced the older parallel style.

entries.name: Alquerque
entries.origin_note: Recorded in the Arab world from the 10th century and in Spain from the 13th century; surviving boards across Spain and North Africa show a long tradition.
entries.summary: Alquerque is a board game of capture played on a grid of 25 points joined by lines, and it is one of the ancestors of draughts. The name comes from the Arabic al-qirkat. It was widely played across Spain and North Africa in the Middle Ages and was described in Alfonso X of Castile's Book of Games, compiled in 1283, which shows the game of twelve pieces a side. Some scholars suggest its roots lie in the ancient Middle East, but there is no reliable dating.
entries.how_played: Each player has twelve pieces, which start on opposite halves of the board with the centre point empty. On a turn, a piece steps along a line to an adjacent empty point, forward or sideways but never backward. A piece captures by jumping over an adjacent enemy piece, in any direction along a line, into the empty point beyond and removing it, and multiple jumps may be chained. Capture is compulsory, and the player who captures all of the opponent's pieces or leaves them with no move wins.
entries.heritage_note: Alquerque boards were scratched into floors, steps and the lids of chests, and played with pebbles and shells by anyone who could draw a few lines. After the Moors came to Spain, the game spread into the rest of Europe, and when players began using chess boards for alquerque with pieces on dark squares only, the result was draughts, in the twelfth century. The game still survives in Spain and the Maghreb in its original form, and the 25-point board can be found in several places as a quiet reminder of the journeys of a game between three continents.

entries.name: Chinese Rings
entries.origin_note: Traditionally attributed to China, with a legend linking it to the general Zhuge Liang of the 3rd century; documented in Europe from the 1500s.
entries.summary: The Chinese Rings puzzle is a mechanical puzzle in which a row of metal rings is linked to a long bar or loop, and the aim is to remove them all. In China it is called jiu lian huan, the nine linked rings, and a popular story says it was devised by the strategist Zhuge Liang to occupy his wife while he was away at war. In Europe it is known as the baguenaudier, which means time-waster, and the Italian mathematician Gerolamo Cardano described it in 1550, so it is sometimes called Cardan's rings.
entries.how_played: Each ring is threaded on a post that passes through the next, and all of them hang from a single bar. The first ring, at the free end of the bar, can always be taken off or put back. Any other ring may be taken off or put on only when the ring immediately before it is on and every ring before that is off. The player must therefore remove and replace rings in a particular order, and a set of nine rings needs 341 moves for the shortest solution.
entries.heritage_note: The puzzle was known in northern English households as tiring irons and in France as baguenaudier, and in each place it passed from parent to child and was often made by local blacksmiths. It proved of interest to mathematicians, and in 1872 the French mathematician Louis Gros described its solution in terms of a binary code now called the Gray code, in the same way as the Tower of Hanoi. Modern Chinese rings are made of brass or steel and are a feature of traditional toy shops. It is an exercise in patience, and the correct approach is to work backward as often as forward.

entries.name: Fox and Geese
entries.origin_note: Documented in England and Scandinavia from the late Middle Ages, with possible links to the older Norse hunt game known as Halatafl; the 33-point cross board is the classic form of the English and German tradition.
entries.summary: Fox and Geese is a hunt game, one of the oldest kinds of board game in Europe, in which one strong piece, the fox, tries to capture a flock of weaker pieces, the geese, which try to trap it. It has been played on the 33-point cross-shaped board in many countries, under names such as Fuchs und Gaense in Germany and Ræv og Gæs in Denmark, and is also related to older hunt games from Scandinavia. Records show it was familiar in England by the 1500s and it remained a children's and farm-kitchen favourite for centuries.
entries.how_played: One player controls the fox and the other controls a flock of thirteen to seventeen geese. The geese start at one end of the board and may step one point forward or sideways, but never backward. The fox may move one step in any allowed direction and captures by jumping over a goose into the empty point behind it. The geese win by pinning the fox so that it cannot move, and the fox wins by capturing enough geese that they can no longer block it.
entries.heritage_note: Fox and Geese is typically scratched or carved into wood, painted on cloth or drawn on slate, and appears across northern Europe on household boards, in taverns and on school benches. Its balance changes with each rule variation: with the geese allowed diagonal moves or compulsory capture for the fox, the game tips one way or the other, and families developed their own house rules. The same idea of a lone predator against many weaker pieces turns up in Asia and Africa, as in the tiger and goat games, which makes it a good starting point for comparing hunt games around the world.

entries.name: Hare and Hounds
entries.origin_note: Recorded in Britain in the 1800s and probably older; related to hunt games such as Fox and Geese that were played across Europe for centuries.
entries.summary: Hare and Hounds is a small hunt game for two players on a board of only eleven points, in which three hounds try to trap a single hare. It is a traditional pastime in Britain and is named after the outdoor chasing game in which runners follow a trail laid by one of their number. Games of this kind are found throughout the world, and small boards like this one are easy to draw on a table or a slate.
entries.how_played: One player has three hounds and the other has one hare, and each turn a single piece steps along a line to an empty point. The hounds may move only forward or sideways, never backward, and they cannot capture. The hounds win by leaving the hare with no legal move. The hare wins by slipping past the hounds to the far side, or by outlasting them until they can no longer make progress.
entries.heritage_note: Because the board is so small the game has been completely analysed, and the hounds can always force a win if they play correctly, which makes the game a gentle exercise in careful planning and teamwork rather than a long struggle. The name was borrowed from the running game that became a fixture of Victorian English schools and gave its name to cross-country clubs such as the Thames Hare and Hounds, founded in 1868. In Britain the board game was played at home by children, and variants with other numbers of hounds and different board shapes appear in books of traditional games.

entries.name: Ludus Latrunculorum
entries.origin_note: Played across the Roman world from about the 1st century BCE to the 5th century CE, with the main sources in Latin literature and archaeological finds of boards and counters across Italy, Britain and the Mediterranean provinces.
entries.summary: Ludus Latrunculorum, the 'game of little soldiers' or 'mercenaries', was one of the best-loved board games of ancient Rome, played from the late Republic to the later Empire. Roman writers including Varro, Ovid and Martial mention it, and an anonymous first-century poem in praise of a nobleman describes a game in vivid detail, from sacrificing pieces to ambushes and recoveries. The complete rules were never written down in a surviving form, so modern players use reconstructions based on these accounts and on the many boards and pieces found across the empire.
entries.how_played: Each player has a force of ordinary soldiers and a single leader, the dux, set out in rows on a board of squares. Pieces move in straight lines, horizontally or vertically, over empty squares. An enemy soldier is captured by trapping it between two of your pieces on opposite sides, and a piece that moves between two enemies of its own accord is safe. The game is won by capturing the enemy force or by trapping what remains so that it cannot move.
entries.heritage_note: Boards have been found from northern Britain to the eastern provinces, scratched into steps and paving slabs by soldiers and townspeople as well as set into stone, with counters of glass, bone, pottery and stone. It was a game of the thoughtful rather than the lucky, and Roman writers praised players who could plan several moves ahead; the poet Ovid lists it as a game a young person should learn. A well-known passage records that a game could last long enough for players to place bets. The tradition ended with the fall of the western empire, though similar capture games, such as the tafl family of northern Europe, are thought to have been influenced by it.

entries.name: Mehen
entries.origin_note: Attested in Egypt from the Predynastic and Early Dynastic periods, through the Old Kingdom; boards and pieces have also been found in the Levant.
entries.summary: Mehen is an ancient Egyptian board game played on a circular board carved as a coiled snake, with the head at the centre and the body divided into spaces. It takes its name from the serpent of Egyptian myth that coiled around the sun's journey to protect it. The game was popular in the early dynasties and the Old Kingdom, from about 3000 to 2300 BCE, and then disappeared from the record, and it has been found in tombs in Egypt as well as at sites in the Levant.
entries.how_played: Players race pieces shaped as lions and lionesses, with marbles also used in play, from the tail of the snake to the head at the centre. Moves were probably decided by throwing sticks or dice, though the exact method is not known, and pieces move along the segments of the coiled body toward the centre. Reconstructions, based on tomb scenes and the finds of boards, pieces and marbles, use captures that send a rival back to the start. The first to bring home all pieces wins.
entries.heritage_note: Stone mehen boards have been found in cemeteries, and several tomb paintings at Saqqara show people playing the game, usually seated on the ground with the board between them. The game appears in Egyptian funerary texts alongside the senet game, which suggests it carried meaning beyond play. It is one of the oldest board games known and also one of the most puzzling, because the original rules were never written down, and different modern researchers have proposed different reconstructions based on the evidence.

entries.name: Nonogram
entries.origin_note: Invented in Japan in 1987-1988 by Non Ishida and Tetsuya Nishio, and spread worldwide in the 1990s through newspapers, magazines and video games.
entries.summary: The nonogram is a logic picture puzzle in which numbers on the edges of a grid tell the player which cells to fill in, until a hidden picture appears. It was invented in Japan in the late 1980s, independently by Non Ishida, a graphic artist who devised it as a way of lighting windows of a skyscraper, and by the puzzle writer Tetsuya Nishio. British newspapers began publishing them from about 1990, and Nintendo released a console version, Picross, in 1995. It is also known as Paint by Numbers, Griddlers and Hanjie.
entries.how_played: The numbers beside each row and above each column give the lengths of the runs of filled squares in that line, in order, and consecutive runs are separated by at least one empty square. For example the clue 3 1 means a run of three filled cells, then at least one gap, then a single filled cell. The solver uses these clues to work out which squares must be filled and which must stay empty, marking empty ones with a cross. A puzzle is solved when every clue is met and the picture appears, and a well-made puzzle has one unique answer reachable by logic alone.
entries.heritage_note: Nonograms are a modern Japanese contribution to the world's puzzle tradition, standing alongside Sudoku, and they belong to a long Japanese enthusiasm for grid-based puzzle books and magazines. They have been shown to be a type of problem that computer scientists classify as hard in the general case, though human solvers enjoy them in the small and medium sizes. Their pictures range from simple icons to detailed portraits on large grids, and their popularity across continents has grown through newspapers, books and games.

entries.name: Peg solitaire
entries.origin_note: Documented at the French court in the late 1600s, with older origins disputed; spread across Europe in the 1700s and 1800s in French and English board layouts.
entries.summary: Peg solitaire is a one-player jumping puzzle in which pegs are removed from a board of holes by jumping over them until as few as possible remain. It is best known in the French and English forms, the French board having 37 holes and the English board 33 in the shape of a cross. A copperplate engraving made in 1697 shows Anne de Rohan-Chabot, Princess of Soubise, at the French court with a solitaire board, and the philosopher Leibniz wrote about the puzzle in 1710 and noted that it was best understood by working backward from the finish.
entries.how_played: All holes are filled with pegs except one in the centre. A peg may jump in a straight line, horizontally or vertically, over one adjacent peg into an empty hole directly beyond, and the peg jumped over is removed. The aim is to finish with a single peg, and finishing with that peg in the centre hole is the master's solution. On a triangular board the pegs may also jump along both diagonals.
entries.heritage_note: The puzzle became a fashionable pastime of the French aristocracy in the 1600s and spread through Europe as a solitary game for long evenings, for travellers and for convalescents. A popular though unproved legend says it was invented by a prisoner who used pebbles and the holes of a pavement to pass the time. Mathematicians have studied the puzzle for centuries, with questions such as which starting holes can end on which finishing holes, and modern wooden boards and glass marbles are still sold in many countries. It is a game that rewards patience, and it requires no opponent at all.

entries.name: Shut the Box
entries.origin_note: Said to have started as a Norman fishermen's tavern game in the 1100s, the earliest firm records of the box game date from the 19th century in England and France.
entries.summary: Shut the Box is a tavern dice game for one or more players, using a wooden box with a row of numbered tiles that flip down to be 'shut'. It is traditionally said to have begun among fishermen in Normandy in northern France and then to have crossed the Channel to England, where it was played in pubs and homes for generations. Its older English name was Batten Down the Hatches, a nautical phrase that reflects its seafaring reputation.
entries.how_played: The box has nine tiles numbered 1 to 9, all standing open. On a turn the player rolls two dice and adds them, then flips down any open tiles that add up to the total, so a roll of 8 may close the 8, or 5 and 3, or 6 and 2, or 1, 2 and 5. The player keeps rolling and closing tiles until no combination of open tiles can match the roll. The score is the sum of the tiles left open, lower is better, and shutting every tile, the 'shut', is a perfect game.
entries.heritage_note: The game was a staple of English pubs and ships and in time found its way to North America, Germany and other countries, where it is sold under local names. A box of finely made tiles and a pair of bone or wooden dice is a common sight in curiosity shops and family cupboards. Because the choices are real, the player can choose between a safe small tile and a risky large one, and experienced players learn the odds of each sum. The same maths is used in classrooms to teach probability and number bonds to children.

entries.name: Surakarta
entries.origin_note: Traditionally associated with Java in Indonesia and named after the city of Surakarta; the earliest firm records come from the 20th century.
entries.summary: Surakarta is a two-player strategy game on a six-by-six grid whose special feature is a pair of looping tracks that run around the board and circle back through the corners. It is named after the city of Surakarta, also called Solo, in central Java in Indonesia, and the game has also been published in Europe under the name Roundabout. The history of its early play is thinly documented, but the game has become a favourite of strategy-game collectors for its striking board.
entries.how_played: Each player has twelve pieces, placed on the two rows nearest to them. A piece may step one point in any direction, including diagonally, onto an empty point. To capture, a piece must travel along one of the two circuits, passing through at least one of the curved corner loops, over empty points and any number of its own side's vacated points, and land on an enemy piece. The captured piece is removed, and the player who takes all of the opponent's pieces wins.
entries.heritage_note: The board's circuits are drawn as two bold circles, called the inner and outer rings, in contrasting colours, and the tension between the quiet, cautious step moves and the sweeping long-range captures gives the game its character. Javanese court culture is known for its refined arts, and a board game named after one of its great cities fits within that heritage. The game is played today in Indonesia and by hobbyists abroad, in particular as a game that rewards seeing a long path before the opponent does.

entries.name: Tennis
entries.origin_note: Patented in London in 1874 by Walter Clopton Wingfield and refined by the All England Club in 1877; descended from the medieval French and English court game now called real tennis.
entries.summary: Lawn tennis was born in England in the 1870s, when Major Walter Clopton Wingfield patented a portable game for gardens that he called Sphairistike, and Birmingham and Leamington enthusiasts created their own versions. It was adapted from the much older indoor game of real tennis, which French and English courts had played since the Middle Ages. The first Wimbledon championship was held in 1877 at the All England Croquet and Lawn Tennis Club, and by the end of the century the game had spread across the world.
entries.how_played: Two players, or two pairs, stand on opposite sides of a net and hit the ball over it, within the lines, so that the opponent cannot return it. Points in a game are counted 15, 30 and 40, a convention inherited from earlier court games, and a player must win by two clear points. A set is won by taking six games with a lead of two, with a tiebreak played at six games all. The match is the best of three or five sets, and the court may be grass, clay or a hard surface, each of which changes the speed and bounce.
entries.heritage_note: Tennis is now played by tens of millions around the world, and its four major tournaments, at Melbourne, Paris, Wimbledon and New York, set its calendar. Grass courts, clay courts and hard courts each reward different styles, and players speak of a surface as having its own character. Wimbledon retains traditions such as an all-white dress code and strawberries and cream, and a long list of champions of many nations has made tennis one of the first global sports. The rules have been remarkably stable since 1877, apart from the introduction of the tiebreak in the 1970s.

entries.name: Tower of Hanoi
entries.origin_note: Invented and patented in Paris in 1883 by Edouard Lucas, a French mathematician, and sold under a Tonkin-inspired fictional legend.
entries.summary: The Tower of Hanoi was invented in 1883 by the French mathematician Edouard Lucas, who published it under the pseudonym 'N. Claus de Siam', an anagram of 'Lucas d'Amiens', after his home town. It was sold as a toy with a printed legend of 64 golden discs moved by patient attendants in a far-off tower, and the name refers to Hanoi, then a city of French Indochina. Lucas was a leader of the recreational mathematics movement, and the puzzle quickly became a favourite of teachers and parents.
entries.how_played: Three pegs stand in a row, and a stack of discs of different sizes starts on the first, with the smallest on top. The player must move the whole stack to another peg, one disc at a time, never placing a larger disc on a smaller one. The smallest number of moves for a stack of n discs is 2 to the power n, minus 1, so three discs need 7 moves, and the legendary 64 would need about 18 quintillion. The strategy is to move the stack above the largest disc away, move that disc, then rebuild on top of it.
entries.heritage_note: The puzzle is among the most studied in mathematics and computing. It is a standard classroom example of recursion, because the solution for n discs uses the solution for n minus 1 discs twice. Its sequence of moves follows the binary Gray code, and psychologists have used it to study planning and problem solving in children and in patients recovering from brain injury. Wooden versions with coloured discs are sold around the world, and it has appeared in stories and films as a symbol of patient, step-by-step effort.

entries.name: Diabolo
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Celtic and Atlantic Europe.
entries.summary: A juggling toy of a spool tossed and spun on a string held by two sticks, popular in France and elsewhere in Europe.
entries.how_played: The player whips the string between two hand sticks to spin the spool, tossing and catching it in tricks.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of France.

entries.name: Sheepdog trials
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Classical Worlds (about 1000 BCE to 500 CE), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Celtic and Atlantic Europe.
entries.summary: Competitions of herding dogs guiding sheep around a field course through gates and into a pen on the shepherd's calls.
entries.how_played: The handler directs a dog by whistles and calls to move a small flock through a set course against the clock.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United Kingdom. Animals are partners in this tradition; good care and local rules always come first.

entries.name: Table football
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Crossroads and Golden Ages (about 500 to 1500), although its exact origins are uncertain.
entries.summary: A tabletop version of football with rods of figures that players spin and slide to strike a small ball.
entries.how_played: Players turn rods holding small figures to hit the ball past the opposing figures into the goal.
entries.heritage_note: A tradition shared by communities in many places.

entries.name: Kongzhu
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of China.
entries.summary: A hollow double-headed whistling spool that is spun and tossed on a string held between two sticks, popular in northern city parks.
entries.how_played: The player whips the string to spin the spool up, then flips it, catches it on the string and performs tricks such as throws and passes behind the body.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of China.

entries.name: Dragon boat racing
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Crossroads and Golden Ages (about 500 to 1500), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of China.
entries.summary: Long narrow paddled boats with a carved dragon head race in teams, set to a drummer's beat.
entries.how_played: Teams of paddlers paddle in unison to a drum while a steersperson guides the boat down a river course.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of China.

entries.name: Taiko
entries.origin_note: A living tradition passed from person to person; it is not tied to a single dated origin. It belongs to the cultural world of Japan and Korea.
entries.summary: A family of Japanese drums played in ensembles with large barrel drums and a kinetic stage style.
entries.how_played: Performers strike drums of different sizes with thick sticks in coordinated rhythms.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Japan.

entries.name: Kintsugi
entries.origin_note: A living tradition passed from person to person; it is not tied to a single dated origin. It belongs to the cultural world of Japan and Korea.
entries.summary: The craft of repairing broken ceramics with lacquer dusted with gold or other metallic powder.
entries.how_played: Fragments are joined with lacquer, cured over time and finished with metallic powder along the seam.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Japan.

entries.name: Bonsai
entries.origin_note: A living tradition passed from person to person; it is not tied to a single dated origin. It belongs to the cultural world of Japan and Korea.
entries.summary: The art of cultivating and shaping miniature trees in shallow containers.
entries.how_played: Growers prune roots and branches, wire limbs and shape trees over years to imitate ancient natural forms.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Japan.

photo.author: Order of the Rose (薔薇騎士団)

entries.name: American patchwork quilting
entries.origin_note: A living tradition passed from person to person; it is not tied to a single dated origin. It belongs to the cultural world of The Americas: North America.
entries.summary: A tradition of stitching small pieces of fabric into patterned tops that are then layered and quilted.
entries.how_played: Quilters cut and sew pieces into blocks, then stitch through layers of cloth.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United States.

entries.name: Pottery
entries.origin_note: A living tradition passed from person to person; it is not tied to a single dated origin.
entries.summary: Shaping clay on a spinning wheel into vessels, practised from ancient Mesopotamia onward.
entries.how_played: Centre the clay on the wheel and pull walls up with the hands.
entries.heritage_note: A tradition shared by communities in many places.

entries.name: Calligraphy
entries.origin_note: A living tradition passed from person to person; it is not tied to a single dated origin.
entries.summary: Decorative handwriting practised in China, Arabic and European traditions.
entries.how_played: Write with brush or pen following set strokes.
entries.heritage_note: A tradition shared by communities in many places.

entries.name: Maze
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain.
entries.summary: A path puzzle with branches and dead ends, drawn or built in many cultures.
entries.how_played: Trace a path from entrance to exit.
entries.heritage_note: A tradition shared by communities in many places.

entries.name: Traditional dhow sail racing
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Age of Contact and Craft (about 1500 to 1800), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Mesopotamia, Levant and Arabia.
entries.summary: Races of traditional wooden sailing boats held in the Gulf.
entries.how_played: Crews race dhows over a set sea course by sail.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United Arab Emirates.

entries.name: Pearl diving
entries.origin_note: A living tradition passed from person to person; it is not tied to a single dated origin. It belongs to the cultural world of Mesopotamia, Levant and Arabia.
entries.summary: Hand-diving for pearl oysters, a main seasonal industry of the Gulf before oil.
entries.how_played: Divers with nose clip and stone weight descend and collect oysters while hauled up by a rope partner.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Bahrain.

entries.name: Kora
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Classical Worlds (about 1000 BCE to 500 CE), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Africa: Sahel, West and Central.
entries.summary: A 21-string bridge harp-lute with a large calabash body, associated with Mande hereditary musicians of the Senegambia region.
entries.how_played: A 21-string bridge harp-lute with a large calabash body, associated with Mande hereditary musicians of the Senegambia region.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Gambia.

entries.name: Rithmomachia
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Crossroads and Golden Ages (about 500 to 1500), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Mediterranean.
entries.summary: Medieval European mathematical board game in which captures depend on the numbers inscribed on pieces.
entries.how_played: Pieces with numbers capture by arithmetic relations and a win comes from forming a victory progression.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Italy.

entries.name: Chinese Checkers
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Deep Past and First Games (before about 3000 BCE), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Northern and Eastern Europe.
entries.summary: Star-shaped board race game, of German origin, for two to six players played individually or in teams.
entries.how_played: Players hop or step marbles across the star board to reach the opposite corner first.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Germany.

photo.author: The original uploader was Hephaestos at English Wikipedia .

entries.name: Bulls and Cows
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Age of Contact and Craft (about 1500 to 1800), although its exact origins are uncertain.
entries.summary: Code-breaking pencil-and-paper game in which one player tries to guess another's secret number.
entries.how_played: One player sets a secret number and the other guesses; each guess is scored by how many digits are right and in place.
entries.heritage_note: A tradition shared by communities in many places. Animals are partners in this tradition; good care and local rules always come first.

entries.name: Vitti Dandu
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Age of Contact and Craft (about 1500 to 1800), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of South Asia.
entries.summary: The Marathi name and local style of gilli-danda, with a small guchhi hole in the centre of the field and its own state federation.
entries.how_played: A short pointed stick is levered out of a small hole with a longer stick and struck in flight; the score depends on the distance reached and whether fielders can catch it.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of India.

entries.name: Traditional football
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Celtic and Atlantic Europe.
entries.summary: Association football, the world's most played sport, was codified in England in 1863 from older village and school kicking games and is now played in every country.
entries.how_played: Two teams move a ball with any part of the body except the hands and arms, trying to kick it into the opposing goal. The full game is eleven a side on a large pitch; seven a side on a compact pitch is the common recreational form.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United Kingdom.

entries.name: Ttakji-ssaum
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Classical Worlds (about 1000 BCE to 500 CE), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Japan and Korea.
entries.summary: A children's contest in which flowers of the violet are hooked together and pulled apart so that the head breaks off one.
entries.how_played: Each child hooks violets by the stems and tugs; the one whose flower head comes off loses.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of South Korea. It is presented as sport and skill, never as real fighting.

entries.name: Jackstraws
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of The Americas: North America.
entries.summary: A game of splints piled on the back of the hand, found among Eskimo and Haida, played like jackstraws.
entries.how_played: Players pile fifty to seventy-five small wooden splints and remove them one at a time without disturbing the rest.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United States.

entries.name: Soroban
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Japan and Korea.
entries.summary: The soroban is the Japanese bead abacus: rods in a wooden frame, each carrying one five-bead above the beam and four one-beads below it, still taught to schoolchildren for fast arithmetic.
entries.how_played: Each rod stands for one decimal place. A number is set by sliding beads toward the beam; adding and subtracting follow fixed finger movements that use the complements of five and ten, so long columns can be summed at speed. Trained users go on to anzan, picturing the beads and calculating entirely in the head.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Japan.

entries.name: American football
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of The Americas: North America.
entries.summary: American football grew out of rugby and association football on the college fields of the north-eastern United States in the 1870s, and became the country's most watched sport.
entries.how_played: Two teams advance an oval ball down a 100-yard field by running or passing, needing ten yards in four downs to keep possession; a touchdown is worth six points and a field goal three. Seven-on-seven is the non-contact practice form, all passing, played on a short field.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United States.

entries.name: Anansi stories
entries.origin_note: A living tradition passed from person to person; it is not tied to a single dated origin. It belongs to the cultural world of Africa: Sahel, West and Central.
entries.summary: Anansesem, the spider stories of the Akan people of Ghana, follow Anansi, a small trickster who wins against bigger and stronger animals by wit, and sometimes loses to his own greed.
entries.how_played: A storyteller performs the tales at evening gatherings, with call-and-response, songs and voices for each animal. Listeners already know the characters, so the pleasure is in the telling and in the lesson each trick carries. The stories crossed the Atlantic and live on in Caribbean and American folklore.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Ghana.

entries.name: Badminton
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Celtic and Atlantic Europe.
entries.summary: Badminton, a racket game played with a feathered shuttlecock over a high net, took its modern rules from British officers in India in the 1870s and is now dominated by players from Indonesia, China, Denmark and India.
entries.how_played: Singles or doubles rally a shuttlecock across a net 1.55 metres high. Games are played to 21 points, best of three, mixing fast smashes with delicate drops at the net.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United Kingdom, India, Indonesia.

entries.name: Baseball
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of The Americas: North America.
entries.summary: Baseball, the bat-and-ball game of nine-player teams and a diamond of four bases, took shape in the north-eastern United States in the 1840s and became a national passion in Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Japan as well.
entries.how_played: A pitcher throws to a batter, who tries to hit the ball into fair territory and run the bases; the fielding side gets three outs per innings and a game lasts nine innings. The home-run contest is a festival form in which hitters simply try to clear the fence as often as they can.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United States, Cuba, Dominican Republic.

entries.name: Basketball
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of The Americas: North America.
entries.summary: Basketball was invented in 1891 in Springfield, Massachusetts, as an indoor winter game with a ball and two peach baskets, and spread from school gyms to city courts around the world.
entries.how_played: Teams score by shooting the ball through a hoop three metres above the floor; players advance by passing or dribbling and may not run holding the ball. Half-court three-on-three, with one basket and a twelve-second shot clock, is the street form and an Olympic event since 2020.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United States.

entries.name: Klondike
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Age of Contact and Craft (about 1500 to 1800), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of The Americas: North America.
entries.summary: Klondike is the best-known solitaire card game, named after the gold rush of the 1890s and played by one person with a single pack.
entries.how_played: Seven columns are dealt with only the top card face up. Cards are built downward in alternating colours on the columns and upward by suit on four foundations, drawing from the remaining stock; the game is won when all four suits are complete.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United States, Canada.

entries.name: Crossword
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), within the cultural world of Celtic and Atlantic Europe.
entries.summary: The crossword puzzle first appeared in a New York newspaper in 1913 and within a decade was a daily habit in Britain and America, where the cryptic style developed.
entries.how_played: A grid of white and black squares is filled with words running across and down, each answering a numbered clue. American grids are dense and fully interlocking; British cryptic clues hide the answer in wordplay as well as a definition.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United Kingdom, United States.

entries.name: Crown Fields
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today).
entries.summary: The solver places crowns by deduction alone.
entries.how_played: The solver places crowns by deduction alone. A region that is one square wide fixes a crown at once; the rows and columns it occupies are then cleared, and the chain of eliminations continues until every region holds exactly one crown.
entries.heritage_note: An Arcforge original, created for the World Heritage Games collection rather than drawn from one tradition.

entries.name: Gamelan
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Classical Worlds (about 1000 BCE to 500 CE), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Southeast Asia and the Islands.
entries.summary: Gamelan is the bronze percussion ensemble of Java and Bali: tuned metallophones, hanging gongs, kettle gongs and drums played together as one instrument.
entries.how_played: The pieces are tuned to each other in the five-tone slendro or seven-tone pelog scales, so no two gamelans sound alike. A large gong marks the end of each cycle, the drum leads the tempo, and layers of metallophones fill the cycle with interlocking patterns.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Indonesia.

entries.name: The Road to Lanka
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), within the cultural world of South Asia.
entries.summary: The Road to Lanka is an Arcforge story adventure drawn from the ancient Sanskrit epic storytelling tradition of South Asia: a prince's long journey south to an island kingdom, told chapter by chapter.
entries.how_played: The player follows the road from the forest exile to the final crossing of the sea, meeting allies and rivals from the epic in turn, with choices at each halt that change how the story is told.
entries.heritage_note: An Arcforge original, created for the World Heritage Games collection rather than drawn from one tradition.

entries.name: Golden Sling
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today).
entries.summary: Golden Sling is an Arcforge original: a harvest field, a hand-carved slingshot and a flock of birds to outwit before they strip the crop. Four seasons bring four guardians to a paper-cut landscape.
entries.how_played: Stones are launched from the sling to scatter the birds before they reach the standing grain; each season changes the wind, the light and the flock.
entries.heritage_note: An Arcforge original, created for the World Heritage Games collection rather than drawn from one tradition.

entries.name: Kolam
entries.origin_note: A living tradition passed from person to person; it is not tied to a single dated origin. It belongs to the cultural world of South Asia.
entries.summary: Kolam is the South Indian art of drawing geometric patterns at the threshold each dawn with rice flour, looping continuous lines around a grid of dots.
entries.how_played: A grid of dots is laid first; then a single line, or a few, is drawn around and between the dots so that every dot is enclosed and the line closes on itself. Designs are learned from mothers and grandmothers and vary by season and occasion.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of India.

entries.name: Miniature golf
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Celtic and Atlantic Europe.
entries.summary: Miniature golf shrinks the putting green into a course of short holes with banks, tunnels and water, a seaside and roadside pastime since the early twentieth century.
entries.how_played: Players putt a ball from a tee to a hole on each of nine or eighteen small greens, counting strokes; obstacles and slopes make each hole a small physics problem.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United Kingdom, United States.

entries.name: One Arrow Oath
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), within the cultural world of South Asia.
entries.summary: One Arrow Oath is an Arcforge original inspired by a warrior's vow in ancient Sanskrit epic poetry: a single arrow, a long campaign and a fresh hand of choices on every attempt.
entries.how_played: Each run strings together encounters from the campaign; the player builds a small deck of techniques and spends them wisely, because the one arrow may be loosed only once.
entries.heritage_note: An Arcforge original, created for the World Heritage Games collection rather than drawn from one tradition.

entries.name: Perch
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today).
entries.summary: Perch is an Arcforge original reflex game: a small bird on a thin perch, stones falling from above and one good moment to move.
entries.how_played: The bird hops left or right to avoid each falling stone; the longer it survives, the faster the stones come.
entries.heritage_note: An Arcforge original, created for the World Heritage Games collection rather than drawn from one tradition.

entries.name: Reversi
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Crossroads and Golden Ages (about 500 to 1500), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Celtic and Atlantic Europe.
entries.summary: Reversi, the disc-flipping game of trapping lines of the opponent's pieces, began in Victorian England in the 1880s and was revived and refined in Japan in the 1970s.
entries.how_played: Two players place double-sided discs on an eight-by-eight board; a disc must be placed so that it traps one or more enemy discs in a straight line, which then flip to the mover's colour. When the board is full the player with more discs wins.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United Kingdom, Japan.

entries.name: Rice terrace farming
entries.origin_note: A living tradition passed from person to person; it is not tied to a single dated origin. It belongs to the cultural world of Southeast Asia and the Islands.
entries.summary: The stone-walled rice terraces of the Philippine Cordillera and the shared-water rice fields of Bali are communal works of engineering: spring water is led downhill through channels and gates so that every field floods and drains in its turn.
entries.how_played: Farmers follow a calendar of planting, flooding, weeding and harvest set by the community, and the irrigation council of each valley decides when each group of fields may take water.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Philippines, Indonesia.

entries.name: Russian Loto
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Crossroads and Golden Ages (about 500 to 1500), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Northern and Eastern Europe.
entries.summary: Russian Loto is the family number lottery of Russia and the former Soviet lands, played with numbered wooden kegs drawn from a cloth bag and cards of three rows.
entries.how_played: Each player buys one or more cards of fifteen numbers. A caller draws kegs one at a time and announces the number, often with a traditional nickname; players cover matches, and the first to fill a row, or the whole card, wins the pot.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Russia.

entries.name: Silk Road caravan trade
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Classical Worlds (about 1000 BCE to 500 CE), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of China.
entries.summary: For more than a thousand years caravans carried silk, paper, glass, spices and horses along the overland routes between Chang'an and Baghdad, trading from oasis to oasis rather than end to end.
entries.how_played: A merchant buys goods where they are cheap, pays for camels, guides and protection, and sells where they are scarce, judging weather, bandits and the politics of each khanate on the way.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of China, Uzbekistan, Iran.

entries.name: Sudoku
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), within the cultural world of Japan and Korea.
entries.summary: Sudoku, the number-placement puzzle, was published in the United States in 1979, named and popularised in Japan in the 1980s and became a worldwide newspaper fixture after 2004.
entries.how_played: A nine-by-nine grid, divided into nine boxes, is partly filled with digits. The solver completes it so that every row, column and box contains the digits one to nine exactly once, by logic alone.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of Japan.

entries.name: Minesweeper
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today).
entries.summary: Minesweeper is a computer-age logic classic from the 1980s: a hidden field of mines must be cleared square by square using only the numbers revealed at each step.
entries.how_played: from these counts the player deduces which neighbours are safe and marks the rest. Sure Sweep is the Arcforge version, built so that no board ever needs a guess.
entries.heritage_note: A tradition shared by communities in many places.

entries.name: Table tennis
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Age of Contact and Craft (about 1500 to 1800), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Celtic and Atlantic Europe.
entries.summary: Table tennis began as an after-dinner parlour game in Victorian England and grew into one of the most played sports on earth, with China dominating competition since the 1960s.
entries.how_played: Two or four players strike a light celluloid or plastic ball across a low net on a table, letting it bounce once on their side; spin and placement matter more than power. Games are played to eleven points.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United Kingdom, China.

entries.name: Cricket
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Age of Contact and Craft (about 1500 to 1800), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of Celtic and Atlantic Europe.
entries.summary: Cricket, the bat-and-ball game of two elevens, a 22-yard pitch and three-stump wickets, grew up in south-east England and travelled with the Commonwealth to South Asia, Australia, southern Africa and the Caribbean.
entries.how_played: A bowler delivers the ball to a batter who defends the wicket and scores runs by hitting and running between the creases; the fielding side tries to dismiss ten batters. Backyard and street cricket keep the game alive with improvised rules everywhere it is played.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United Kingdom, India, Australia.

entries.name: Volleyball
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today), although its exact origins are uncertain, within the cultural world of The Americas: North America.
entries.summary: Volleyball was devised in Massachusetts in 1895 as a gentler indoor game than basketball and became a worldwide team sport, with beach volleyball following from California in the 1920s.
entries.how_played: Six a side send the ball over a high net with no more than three touches, usually pass, set and spike, and rotate positions after each point won on serve. Rallies end when the ball touches the floor or goes out.
entries.heritage_note: Part of the living heritage of United States, Brazil, Japan.

entries.name: Word Game
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today).
entries.summary: Players study a set of words, then are tested on them in short timed rounds that return to the words they missed.
entries.how_played: Players study a set of words, then are tested on them in short timed rounds that return to the words they missed.
entries.heritage_note: An Arcforge original, created for the World Heritage Games collection rather than drawn from one tradition.

entries.name: World Weave
entries.origin_note: Usually placed in the era of Modern Heritage (1800 to today).
entries.summary: World Weave is an Arcforge original pattern puzzle that weaves real textile and tile traditions from many civilizations into one loom.
entries.how_played: Each pattern is rebuilt thread by thread from the motifs of its home tradition, following the lineage of the design rather than any one country.
entries.heritage_note: An Arcforge original, created for the World Heritage Games collection rather than drawn from one tradition.
